content: Sudan staining involves the application of Sudan dyes to identify sudanophilic substances, primarily lipids. Sudan lysochromes, such as Sudan II, Sudan III, Sudan IV, Oil Red O, and Sudan Black B, are commonly employed for this purpose. These dyes exhibit a strong affinity for fats, making them effective in detecting triglycerides, lipids, and lipoproteins. Typically, Sudan dyes are dissolved in alcoholic solutions for use, although pyridine-based solutions may be utilized in specific cases. The Sudan stain test is frequently employed to assess fecal fat levels, aiding in the diagnosis of steatorrhea. In this procedure, a small stool sample is dissolved in water or saline, and glacial acetic acid is added to hydrolyze insoluble fatty acid salts. Subsequently, a few drops of an alcoholic solution of Sudan III are introduced. The sample is then spread onto a microscopic slide and heated to boiling twice. Under normal conditions, a stool sample should reveal only a minimal number of red-orange stained fat droplets when examined microscopically. Although the method is only semiquantitative, its simplicity makes it a valuable tool for initial screening purposes.
